[Page 545]

Rhetorical interrogative (istifham taqriri, a question that seeks affirmation). I have explained on more than one occasion that the rhetorical interrogative often takes the form of a negation, with the affirmation of what is established, for the sake of certainty. The one being affirmed can only accept the affirmation of what is negated. See the commentary on the words of God Most High: ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:243] in Surat al-Baqarah. The rhetorical interrogative here is a metaphor (majaz) based on a relationship of necessary consequence (ʿalaqat al-luzum). This metaphor has been used so frequently in their speech that, because of its currency, it has come to function like a literal meaning (haqiqa). Accordingly, the affirmation is used metaphorically to express honour, indicating that this event was a foreshadowing (irhas) of the Prophet ﷺ. It is therefore of the same type as His words: ﴿I swear by this city﴾ [al-Balad 90:1] ﴿while you are a resident of this city﴾ [al-Balad 90:2].

[Page 545 continued]

Along with this, there is an implicit reproach (taʿrid) to the Quraysh for their ingratitude for a great blessing of God upon them, since they continued to worship other than Him.

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, as his words "your Lord" (rabbuka) require. The general sense of this verse is similar to His words: ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?﴾ [al-Duha 93:6] and the verses that follow it, and to His words: ﴿I swear by this city﴾ [al-Balad 90:1] ﴿while you are a resident of this city﴾ [al-Balad 90:2], according to one of the aspects mentioned earlier.

The verb "seeing" (al-ru'ya) may be metaphorical, borrowed to mean knowledge that has reached the level of certainty equal to seeing something with the eyes, because of the widespread transmission of what God did to the People of the Elephant among the people of Makkah, and because some traces of it remained that they could observe. Abu Salih said: "I saw in the house of Umm Hani bint Abi Talib about two qafiz [a measure] of those stones, black and streaked with red." ʿAtab ibn Asid said: "I met the groom of the elephant and its driver, both blind and crippled, begging from people." ʿAisha said: "I certainly saw the driver of the elephant and its leader, both blind, begging from people." The verb of seeing is suspended (muʿallaq) by the interrogative.

It may also be that the seeing is visual (basariyya), in relation to those who were more than fifty years old at the time the verse was revealed, from among those who witnessed the event of the Elephant as boys or young men, such as Abu Quhafa, Abu Talib, and Ubayy ibn Khalaf.

The word "how" (kayfa) is an interrogative that takes the place of two objects or the object of "you saw" (tara). That is, "Have you not seen the answer to this question," just as you say: "I know whether Zayd is standing." It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the subject of "you saw". It is also possible that kayfa is stripped of the meaning of interrogation and intended merely to express the manner (kayfiyya), in which case it is in the accusative as the direct object.

The choice of kayfa over other interrogative or relative words, such that it is not said "Have you not seen what your Lord did" or "that which your Lord did," serves to indicate a wondrous state which those who know the details of the story will call to mind.

The expression "your Lord did" (fa'ala rabbuka) was chosen over others because the meaning of this verb encompasses many actions which no other verb indicates.

In defining God, the Exalted, the description "Lord" (Rabb) is used in construct with the pronoun of the Prophet ﷺ, [Page 546] as a hint that the purpose of reminding about this story is to honour the Prophet ﷺ as a foreshadowing of his prophethood, since that occurred in the year of his birth.

The People of the Elephant (ashab al-fil) were the Abyssinians who came to Makkah as invaders, intending to demolish the Kaʿba in retaliation against the Arabs because of what a member of the Banu Kinana had done. The Banu Kinana were the ones who practised the intercalation (al-nasiʾ) in the sacred months of the Hajj. The account and its cause were as follows: the Abyssinians had taken control of Yemen after the event of al-Ukhdud, in which the king Dhu Nuwas tortured the Christians. The Abyssinian governor over Yemen became a man called Abraha. Abraha built a great church in Sanaa, which he called al-Qalis (the vowel of the first letter is fatha, the second is kasra followed by a silent ya; some pronounce it with damma on the first letter, fatha on the lam, and a silent ya; in the Qamus it is given with damma on the qaf and a shadda on the lam with fatha, and a silent ya; al-Suhayli wrote it with a nun after the lam and did not vowel it, and claimed it was a name derived from the meanings of "qals," meaning elevation, from which comes "qalansuwa" [cap]; he limited himself to this and I do not know the origin of this word. It may be a generic name for a church, and perhaps the word kanisa in Arabic is arabicised from it, or it may be a proper name which they gave to this particular church). Abraha wanted to divert the pilgrimage of the Arabs to it instead of the Kaʿba. It is narrated that a man from the Banu Fuqaym of the Banu Kinana, who were the people of intercalation for the Arabs, as previously mentioned in the commentary on His words: ﴿The postponement is only an increase in disbelief﴾ [al-Tawba 9:37] in Surat Bara'a, went to Sanaa until he came to al-Qalis and defiled it, intending to belittle it so that the Arabs would hear of it. Abraha became angry and resolved to invade Makkah to demolish the Kaʿba. He marched until he camped outside Makkah at night in a place called al-Mughammas (on the pattern of mu'azzam), a location near Makkah on the road to al-Ta'if, or Dhu al-Ghamis (I have not seen its vocalisation). He sent to ʿAbd al-Muttalib to warn him not to fight them, and a conversation took place between them. ʿAbd al-Muttalib ordered his family and all the people of Makkah to leave the city for the surrounding mountains, fearing the harm of the army if they entered Makkah. When morning came, he prepared his army to enter Makkah. Abraha was riding an elephant with his army accompanying him. While he was preparing for this, a fatal disease, the deadly smallpox, afflicted his soldiers, causing their fingertips to fall off. Before that, they had seen birds throwing stones at them, which would not strike anyone without killing him; these were birds from the army of God. Most of the army perished, and some of them turned back. Abraha fell ill and returned to Sanaa sick, and he died in Sanaa. God spared the people of Makkah the affair of their enemy. This happened in the month of Muharram, corresponding to the month of Shubat (February), in the year 570 after the birth of Jesus, peace be upon him, and fifty days after this event the Prophet ﷺ was born, according to the most authentic reports, though there is considerable disagreement about this.

The definite article in "the elephant" (al-fil) is for a known reference (ʿahd), and it refers to the elephant of Abraha, the army commander, just as they called the army that went out with ʿAisha, the Mother of the Believers, "the People of the Camel" (ashab al-jamal), meaning the camel on which ʿAisha was riding, even though there were other camels in the army. It has been said that Abraha's army had only one elephant, that of Abraha, whose name was Mahmud. It has also been said that there were other elephants in it, said to be eight, and said to be twelve. Some said there were a thousand elephants. And there is a verse attributed to ʿAbd al-Muttalib in a rajaz metre:

"You prevented the Abyssinians and the elephants."

In that case the definite article is the definition of the genus (taʿrif al-jins), and the known reference is derived from the construct (idafa).

The elephant (al-fil) is a great animal among the quadrupeds with hooves, from the fauna of hot lands with rivers, such as India, China, Abyssinia, and Sudan. It is not found outside these regions except when imported. It is intelligent, capable of being tamed and trained, huge in body, larger than the camel, somewhat taller than it, with more flesh and a larger belly. Its hoof resembles the camel's hoof. Its neck is very short. It has a long trunk, which is its nose, with which it takes its food and draws water to pour into its mouth, and with which it defends itself. It seizes with it, twists it on whatever animal it wants to harm, throws it to the ground, and tramples it with its legs. Its eyes are squinting, its ears are large and drooping, and its tail is short, shorter than the camel's tail. Its legs are thick, and its footpads are like those of the camel. The male has two long tusks projecting from its mouth, from which people make ivory. Its skin is hairless, like cowhide, reddish-brown in colour, dark like the colour of a mouse, though there are white-skinned ones. It is ridden and used to carry loads. The people of India and China use the elephant in war like a fortress; they place a litter on its back that holds six soldiers. The elephant was not known among the Arabs, so it rarely occurred in their speech. The first elephant to enter the lands of the Arabs was the elephant mentioned in this sura.

Poetry has been reported about this event in the biography (sira), but the Arabs used to hear reports of the elephant and imagine it great and strong. Labid said:

"And a narrow station that I opened up with eloquence, speech, and argument.
Were the elephant or its keeper to stand, it would slip from a position like mine, and would be unable to bear it."

Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr said in his qasida:

"I stand in a station where, were the elephant to stand in it, it would see and hear what the elephant does not see or hear,
It would keep trembling, unless it had a share from the Messenger by God's permission."

I had thought that... He said that his mother showed him, or told him, that she had seen elephant dung in Makkah around the Kaʿba, and perhaps they left it unremoved so that it would remain as a reminder.

From ʿAisha and ʿAtab ibn Asid: "I saw the driver of the elephant and its keeper in Makkah, both blind and crippled, begging from people."

The meaning is: "Have you not known the wondrous state which God did to the People of the Elephant?" This is a rhetorical affirmation of a general matter which what follows explains.

ألَمْ يَجْعَلْ كَيْدَهم في تَضْلِيلٍ

[Page 549]

These phrases clarify the general statement in ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ [al-Fil: 1]. He called their war a "plot" (kayd) because it was an action whose outward appearance was anger over the act of the Kinani man who sat in the church (al-Qalis), but it was really a pretext they used to create a cause for waging war on the people of Makkah and demolishing the Ka'bah, so that the Arabs would turn toward the pilgrimage to al-Qalis in Sana'a and become Christians.

Or the intended meaning of "their plot" is their building of al-Qalis, while showing that they had built a church, when in fact they wanted to nullify the pilgrimage to the Ka'bah and turn the Arabs toward Sana'a.

Kayd (plot) means scheming to inflict harm on another and working to bring it about.

Tadlil (leading astray) means making another person lost, that is, not guided to his aim. Here it is a metaphor for nullifying and failing to attain the intended goal, because a traveler who loses the road does not reach his destination.

The "in" (fi) of "in tadlil" is figurative: the particle of place (zarfiyyah) is used to express the meaning of accompaniment (musahabah). The meaning is: He nullified their plot together with an error that never left it, i.e., He nullified it completely and severely, since they gained nothing from their strength despite the weakness of the people of Makkah and the smallness of their number. This is like His saying: ﴿And the plot of Pharaoh was not but in ruin﴾ [Ghafir: 37], meaning loss and destruction. The "leading astray of their plot" covered everything that befell them of the causes of failure and an evil outcome.

The clause ﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾ may be taken as coordinated (ma'tufah) with the clause "dealt with" (fa'ala rabbuka bi-ashab al-fil), meaning: "and how He sent against them birds of such and such a description." After the affirmation of what God did to them, in leading their plot astray, there is coordinated with it an affirmation of the knowledge of the punishment He imposed upon them for their plot, as a reminder of what befell them of God's vengeance for their intention to destroy the Ka'bah. This is part of God's care for His House, to show the preparation for the sending of His Messenger ﷺ with His religion in that city, in response to the supplication of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Just as the sending of the birds against them was among the causes of leading their plot astray, it also contained a recompense for them, so that they would know that God protects His House. The clause ﴿Did He not make their plot go astray?﴾ would then be a parenthetical clause between the two coordinated clauses.

It may also be permissible to take ﴿And He sent against them﴾ as coordinated with the clause ﴿Did He not make their plot go astray?﴾, so that it falls within the scope of the second affirmation, namely that God made their plot go astray. He singled this out for mention because it combines two things: that it nullified their plot and that it was a punishment for them. Its coming in the past tense (lafz al-madi) is because the present-tense verb in ﴿Did He not make their plot go astray?﴾ had its time turned into the past by the entry of the particle (lam), as mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge?﴾ [al-Duha: 6] ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ [al-Duha: 7] in Surat al-Duha. It is as if it were said: "Did He not make their plot go astray?"

[Page 550]

Al-tayr (birds) is a noun, the plural of ta'ir, which is the animal that rises into the air by the action of its wings. Its indefiniteness (tankir) is for the sake of indicating a type, because it was a kind that was not known to the Arabs. The storytellers (al-qussas) differed greatly and imaginatively in describing it. The sound view is what is reported from 'A'ishah: that it resembled the swallows (al-khataFif) most, and from others that it resembled the bat (al-watwat).

Ababil means groups. Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Ababil is a collective noun with no singular from its own form, like 'abadid and shamatit." Al-Jawhari followed them both. Al-Ru'asi and al-Zamakhshari said: the singular of ababil is ibbalah, with a doubled ba' and a kasrah on the hamzah. From this comes their proverb: "a bundle upon a bundle" (dighth 'ala ibbalah), and ibbalah is a large bundle of firewood. Accordingly, the description of the birds as ababil is a highly eloquent (baligh) simile.

The clause ﴿they strike them﴾ (tarmihim) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from ﴿birds﴾ (tayran). The present tense is used to make the situation present, so that it is imagined to the listener as an event occurring in the time of the situation. Among examples is His saying: ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and We drive them to a dead land﴾ [Fatir: 9], and so on.

Hijarah (stones) is a collective noun whose singular is hajar.

From Ibn 'Abbas, he said: "clay among stones." Also from him: that sijjil is arabized (mu'arrab) from Persian, from "sang-gil" (sanък kil); that is, from the word "sang" (stone). It is vocalized with a fatha on the sin, a sukun on the nun, and a kasrah on the kaf, and means "stone." The word "gil" with a kasrah on the kaf means "clay." The combination of the two words is meant to refer to baked brick (al-ajurr).

Both words have the Persian kaf that is pointed (al-mu'ammadah), which lies between the articulation point of the kaf and that of the qaf. For this reason "min" (from) is explicative (bayaniyyah), meaning: "stones which are sijjil." Al-Subki counted the word sijjil in his versified work (manzumah) among the arabized words found in the Qur'an.

The origin of its meaning is pointed to by His saying: ﴿that We may send down upon them stones of clay﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 33], together with His saying in other verses: ﴿stones of sijjil﴾ [Hud: 82]. Thus it is known that it is a stone whose origin is clay.

A parallel to it occurs in the story of the people of Lut in Surat Hud: ﴿And We rained upon them stones of sijjil, layered﴾ [Hud: 82], and in Surat al-Hijr: ﴿So We turned it upside down and rained upon them stones of sijjil﴾ [al-Hijr: 74]. Therefore it is established that the stones sent upon the companions of the elephant were of the same kind as the stones rained upon the people of Lut. That is, they were not rock stones, but clay hardened into stone, as a sign that they were created for their punishment.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "When a stone fell upon one of them, his skin blistered, and that was the first smallpox (al-judari)." 'Ikrimah said: "If one of them was struck by one, smallpox would come out on him."

[Page 551]

It has been said that smallpox was not known in Makkah before that.

It is also reported that the stone was the size of a chickpea (al-himmas). Abu Nu'aym related from Nawfal ibn Abi Mu'awiyah al-Daylami, who said: "I saw the pebbles with which the companions of the elephant were struck: pebbles like chickpeas, red, with a blackish (i.e., black) tint, as if they were pieces of Zafari onyx (jiz' Zafari)." From Ibn 'Abbas: that he saw some of these stones with Umm Hani' — about a qafiz of them, streaked with redness, of the Zafari onyx kind.

Al-'asf means the leaves of crops, and it is the plural of 'asfah. When animals enter a field of 'asf and eat it, they trample it with their feet, eat its edges, and throw it onto the ground after it had been green and lush. This is a simile (tamthil) for the state of the companions of the elephant after that freshness and strength: how they became fallen upon the ground, destroyed.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surat Quraysh

This surah was named in the era of the early generations (al-salaf) "Surat li-Ilaf Quraysh" (For the Accustomed Security of Quraysh). 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi said: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab prayed the Maghrib prayer and in the second rak'ah recited ﴿Have you not considered how?﴾ and ﴿For the accustomed security of Quraysh﴾." This clearly indicates the intended naming. He did not count it in al-Itqan among the surahs that have more than one name.

It is named in the mushafs and books of tafsir "Surat Quraysh," because the name Quraysh occurs in it and does not occur in any other surah. On this basis al-Bukhari titled it in his Sahih.

The surah is Meccan according to the majority of scholars. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "without any disagreement." In al-Qurtubi, it is reported from al-Kalbi and al-Dahhak that it is Medinan. He did not mention it in al-Itqan among the surahs on which there is disagreement.

It is counted as the twenty-ninth in the order of the revelation of surahs. It was revealed after Surat al-Tin and before Surat al-Qari'ah.

It is a surah standing on its own by the consensus (ijma') of the Muslims, in that it is a distinct surah.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b joined it with Surat al-Fil as one surah and did not separate them in his mushaf with the basmalah, which they used as a marker of separation between surahs. This is the apparent meaning of the report from 'Amr ibn Maymun about the recitation of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. The consensus that occurred afterward nullified that.

The number of its verses is four according to the majority of counters. The people of Makkah and Madinah counted them as five verses.

I saw in an old mushaf among the manuscript mushafs in al-Qayrawan that its count is four verses, even though the recitation of the people of al-Qayrawan is the recitation of the people of Madinah.

[Page 554]

The command to the Quraysh to affirm Allah's Lordship (rububiyyah), as a reminder to them of the blessing that Allah enabled them to travel the earth for trade in the two journeys of winter and summer, without fearing any enemy who might attack them.

And that He secured them from famine and secured them from fears, because of the reverence for them that was firmly established in the souls of the Arabs, since they were the residents of the Sanctuary (haram) and the builders of the Ka'bah.

And by what He inspired among people of bringing provisions (al-mirah) to them from the neighboring regions, such as the lands of Abyssinia.

And by the repelling of the tribes, so that no one raids their land. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a sanctuary secure while people are being snatched away all around them? Then in falsehood do they believe, and in the favor of Allah do they deny?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 67]. Thus this gave them awe in people's souls and kindness from them.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surat Quraysh

This surah was named in the era of the early generations (al-salaf) "Surat li-Ilaf Quraysh" (For the Accustomed Security of Quraysh). 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi said: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab prayed the Maghrib prayer and in the second rak'ah recited ﴿Have you not considered how?﴾ and ﴿For the accustomed security of Quraysh﴾." This clearly indicates the intended naming. He did not count it in al-Itqan among the surahs that have more than one name.

It is named in the mushafs and books of tafsir "Surat Quraysh," because the name Quraysh occurs in it and does not occur in any other surah. On this basis al-Bukhari titled it in his Sahih.

The surah is Meccan according to the majority of scholars. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "without any disagreement." In al-Qurtubi, it is reported from al-Kalbi and al-Dahhak that it is Medinan. He did not mention it in al-Itqan among the surahs on which there is disagreement.

It is counted as the twenty-ninth in the order of the revelation of surahs. It was revealed after Surat al-Tin and before Surat al-Qari'ah.

It is a surah standing on its own by the consensus (ijma') of the Muslims, in that it is a distinct surah.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b joined it with Surat al-Fil as one surah and did not separate them in his mushaf with the basmalah, which they used as a marker of separation between surahs. This is the apparent meaning of the report from 'Amr ibn Maymun about the recitation of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. The consensus that occurred afterward nullified that.

The number of its verses is four according to the majority of counters. The people of Makkah and Madinah counted them as five verses.

I saw in an old mushaf among the manuscript mushafs in al-Qayrawan that its count is four verses, even though the recitation of the people of al-Qayrawan is the recitation of the people of Madinah.

* * *

[Page 554]

The command to the Quraysh to affirm Allah's Lordship (rububiyyah), as a reminder to them of the blessing that Allah enabled them to travel the earth for trade in the two journeys of winter and summer, without fearing any enemy who might attack them.

And that He secured them from famine and secured them from fears, because of the reverence for them that was firmly established in the souls of the Arabs, since they were the residents of the Sanctuary (haram) and the builders of the Ka'bah.

And by what He inspired among people of bringing provisions (al-mirah) to them from the neighboring regions, such as the lands of Abyssinia.

And by the repelling of the tribes, so that no one raids their land. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a sanctuary secure while people are being snatched away all around them? Then in falsehood do they believe, and in the favor of Allah do they deny?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 67]. Thus this gave them awe in people's souls and kindness from them.

ألَمْ يَجْعَلْ كَيْدَهم في تَضْلِيلٍ

[Page 549]

These phrases clarify the general statement in ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ [al-Fil: 1]. He called their war a "plot" (kayd) because it was an action whose outward appearance was anger over the act of the Kinani man who sat in the church (al-Qalis), but it was really a pretext they used to create a cause for waging war on the people of Makkah and demolishing the Ka'bah, so that the Arabs would turn toward the pilgrimage to al-Qalis in Sana'a and become Christians.

Or the intended meaning of "their plot" is their building of al-Qalis, while showing that they had built a church, when in fact they wanted to nullify the pilgrimage to the Ka'bah and turn the Arabs toward Sana'a.

Kayd (plot) means scheming to inflict harm on another and working to bring it about.

Tadlil (leading astray) means making another person lost, that is, not guided to his aim. Here it is a metaphor for nullifying and failing to attain the intended goal, because a traveler who loses the road does not reach his destination.

The "in" (fi) of "in tadlil" is figurative: the particle of place (zarfiyyah) is used to express the meaning of accompaniment (musahabah). The meaning is: He nullified their plot together with an error that never left it, i.e., He nullified it completely and severely, since they gained nothing from their strength despite the weakness of the people of Makkah and the smallness of their number. This is like His saying: ﴿And the plot of Pharaoh was not but in ruin﴾ [Ghafir: 37], meaning loss and destruction. The "leading astray of their plot" covered everything that befell them of the causes of failure and an evil outcome.

The clause ﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾ may be taken as coordinated (ma'tufah) with the clause "dealt with" (fa'ala rabbuka bi-ashab al-fil), meaning: "and how He sent against them birds of such and such a description." After the affirmation of what God did to them, in leading their plot astray, there is coordinated with it an affirmation of the knowledge of the punishment He imposed upon them for their plot, as a reminder of what befell them of God's vengeance for their intention to destroy the Ka'bah. This is part of God's care for His House, to show the preparation for the sending of His Messenger ﷺ with His religion in that city, in response to the supplication of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Just as the sending of the birds against them was among the causes of leading their plot astray, it also contained a recompense for them, so that they would know that God protects His House. The clause ﴿Did He not make their plot go astray?﴾ would then be a parenthetical clause between the two coordinated clauses.

It may also be permissible to take ﴿And He sent against them﴾ as coordinated with the clause ﴿Did He not make their plot go astray?﴾, so that it falls within the scope of the second affirmation, namely that God made their plot go astray. He singled this out for mention because it combines two things: that it nullified their plot and that it was a punishment for them. Its coming in the past tense (lafz al-madi) is because the present-tense verb in ﴿Did He not make their plot go astray?﴾ had its time turned into the past by the entry of the particle (lam), as mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge?﴾ [al-Duha: 6] ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ [al-Duha: 7] in Surat al-Duha. It is as if it were said: "Did He not make their plot go astray?"

[Page 550]

Al-tayr (birds) is a noun, the plural of ta'ir, which is the animal that rises into the air by the action of its wings. Its indefiniteness (tankir) is for the sake of indicating a type, because it was a kind that was not known to the Arabs. The storytellers (al-qussas) differed greatly and imaginatively in describing it. The sound view is what is reported from 'A'ishah: that it resembled the swallows (al-khataFif) most, and from others that it resembled the bat (al-watwat).

Ababil means groups. Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Ababil is a collective noun with no singular from its own form, like 'abadid and shamatit." Al-Jawhari followed them both. Al-Ru'asi and al-Zamakhshari said: the singular of ababil is ibbalah, with a doubled ba' and a kasrah on the hamzah. From this comes their proverb: "a bundle upon a bundle" (dighth 'ala ibbalah), and ibbalah is a large bundle of firewood. Accordingly, the description of the birds as ababil is a highly eloquent (baligh) simile.

The clause ﴿they strike them﴾ (tarmihim) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from ﴿birds﴾ (tayran). The present tense is used to make the situation present, so that it is imagined to the listener as an event occurring in the time of the situation. Among examples is His saying: ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and We drive them to a dead land﴾ [Fatir: 9], and so on.

Hijarah (stones) is a collective noun whose singular is hajar.

From Ibn 'Abbas, he said: "clay among stones." Also from him: that sijjil is arabized (mu'arrab) from Persian, from "sang-gil" (sanък kil); that is, from the word "sang" (stone). It is vocalized with a fatha on the sin, a sukun on the nun, and a kasrah on the kaf, and means "stone." The word "gil" with a kasrah on the kaf means "clay." The combination of the two words is meant to refer to baked brick (al-ajurr).

Both words have the Persian kaf that is pointed (al-mu'ammadah), which lies between the articulation point of the kaf and that of the qaf. For this reason "min" (from) is explicative (bayaniyyah), meaning: "stones which are sijjil." Al-Subki counted the word sijjil in his versified work (manzumah) among the arabized words found in the Qur'an.

The origin of its meaning is pointed to by His saying: ﴿that We may send down upon them stones of clay﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 33], together with His saying in other verses: ﴿stones of sijjil﴾ [Hud: 82]. Thus it is known that it is a stone whose origin is clay.

A parallel to it occurs in the story of the people of Lut in Surat Hud: ﴿And We rained upon them stones of sijjil, layered﴾ [Hud: 82], and in Surat al-Hijr: ﴿So We turned it upside down and rained upon them stones of sijjil﴾ [al-Hijr: 74]. Therefore it is established that the stones sent upon the companions of the elephant were of the same kind as the stones rained upon the people of Lut. That is, they were not rock stones, but clay hardened into stone, as a sign that they were created for their punishment.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "When a stone fell upon one of them, his skin blistered, and that was the first smallpox (al-judari)." 'Ikrimah said: "If one of them was struck by one, smallpox would come out on him."

[Page 551]

It has been said that smallpox was not known in Makkah before that.

It is also reported that the stone was the size of a chickpea (al-himmas). Abu Nu'aym related from Nawfal ibn Abi Mu'awiyah al-Daylami, who said: "I saw the pebbles with which the companions of the elephant were struck: pebbles like chickpeas, red, with a blackish (i.e., black) tint, as if they were pieces of Zafari onyx (jiz' Zafari)." From Ibn 'Abbas: that he saw some of these stones with Umm Hani' — about a qafiz of them, streaked with redness, of the Zafari onyx kind.

Al-'asf means the leaves of crops, and it is the plural of 'asfah. When animals enter a field of 'asf and eat it, they trample it with their feet, eat its edges, and throw it onto the ground after it had been green and lush. This is a simile (tamthil) for the state of the companions of the elephant after that freshness and strength: how they became fallen upon the ground, destroyed.
